AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery

Shicheng Liu22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Stanford University    Krista Opsahl-Ong Affiliation: Databricks AI Research    Andrew Drozdov Affiliation: Databricks AI Research    Julian Killingback Affiliation: Databricks AI Research Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Amherst    Arnav Singhvi Affiliation: Databricks AI Research    Ronak Pradeep Affiliation: Databricks AI Research    Michael Bendersky Affiliation: Databricks AI Research    James C. Dickerson11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Division of Oncology, Stanford University School of Medicine    Monica S. Lam11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Stanford University
Abstract

Reproducible and analytically robust research findings are essential to scientific progress, but evaluating these properties typically requires costly manual effort. We investigate whether LLM agents can help automate reproduction and robustness analysis, using a medical case study grounded in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, a widely used U.S. cancer registry underlying tens of thousands of published studies. First, we introduce SEER-Repro, a benchmark of 20 published SEER-based papers together with the data and resources required to reproduce their findings. Second, we create an AI agent that successfully reproduces 77.4% of 2,190 atomic claims, while providing executable baselines for further analysis. Third, we develop an agentic analysis pipeline to test the robustness of the medical findings by identifying analytical choices underlying each finding, proposing defensible alternatives, and rerunning the analysis to determine whether those choices affect the conclusion. Across published papers in SEER-Repro, our pipeline identifies potentially consequential analytical choices in 9.5% of fully reproduced findings and flags them for expert review. These results show how LLM agents can support scientific review by reproducing findings, systematically testing their robustness, and directing expert attention toward potentially consequential analytical choices.

1 Introduction

Reproducibility and analytical robustness are the bedrock on which scientific discovery rests. Reproducibility ensures that research findings can be independently verified, while analytical robustness asks whether conclusions remain stable under reasonable alternative choices. Traditionally, meta-analyses and systematic reviews have addressed these challenges through laborious, manual efforts to reproduce experiments or reanalyze data using alternate specifications (Delios and others, 2022; Brodeur et al., 2026). However, the immense cost and expertise required for such metascientific investigations have limited their scalability. Scientific claims also depend on the analytical decisions made by their authors (Simonsohn et al., 2020; Bertran et al., 2026). Recent “many-analyst” studies in psychology and the social sciences show that independent teams addressing the same hypothesis and dataset can reach conflicting conclusions (Silberzahn et al., 2018; Breznau et al., 2022; Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020). Large language models (LLMs) offer a way to explore this analytical diversity at scale. Importantly, these AI-driven results exhibit notable steerability: shifting the design of the analyst persona or changing the underlying LLM meaningfully alters the distribution of analytic outcomes, even when methodological rigor is maintained throughout (Bertran et al., 2026; Miao et al., 2026).

Does this sensitivity to analytical choices documented in psychological and social sciences extend to medicine, where findings profoundly inform clinical decisions and patient care? Addressing this question is critical, as the validity of medical research underpins clinical decisions that affect countless lives. In this paper, we investigate the potential of AI-driven analysts to enhance both reproducibility and analytical robustness in scientific discovery, with a particular focus on medical epidemiology using the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database. Maintained by the National Cancer Institute since 1973, the program integrates population-based cancer-registry records on patient demographics, tumor characteristics, treatment, and survival. In its 2024 usage metrics, NCI reports that 17 core registries cover roughly 48% of the U.S. population and collect approximately 950,000 incident cases per year (National Cancer Institute, 2026e; National Cancer Institute, 2025). From 1975 through 2024, approximately 25,000 publications used SEER data in their primary analysis, while more than 126,000 publications referenced SEER data (National Cancer Institute, 2025). This scale provides a large body of realistic, high-impact questions, while differences in data and analytical definitions, such as registry coverage and cohort selection, make faithful reconstruction challenging.

We argue that, before LLMs can be trusted to produce new scientific results, they must first demonstrate the ability to accurately reproduce existing scientific studies and assess their analytical robustness. Motivated by this prerequisite, this paper addresses two key research questions:

First, can we create an AI agent to reproduce published medical epidemiological studies? And if so, what is the reproducibility rate of such papers? We construct SEER-Repro, the first benchmark consisting of 20 original recent or highly cited papers published on the SEER data. We develop an AI agent to reproduce the results of each paper by reading the paper and database documentation, writing and executing the code to access and process the SEER data accordingly. Across 2,190 atomic claims, our pipeline reproduced 77.4%, while 3.5% were close and 19.2% were not reproduced. Error analysis identifies unavailable data as the main barrier to reproduction, despite extensive efforts to recover all required data.

Second, can we create an AI agent to evaluate the analytical robustness of findings in SEER-Repro? And if so, how robust are those findings to reasonable alternative analytical choices? We formulate the task of analytical robustness evaluation as follows: Given a research report and access to the underlying data, the task is to investigate if there are well-justified analytical choices that can change the conclusions of the report. We refer to such choices as consequential. Evaluating analytical robustness is challenging because gold-standard judgments do not exist. We therefore investigate three complementary approaches: (1) asking a coding agent to independently analyze the data and comparing its conclusions with those of the published paper; (2) systematically perturbing individual analytical choices through a structured agentic pipeline; and (3) asking coding agents to assess analytical robustness directly. To rate how strongly alternative analyses could change published conclusions, we adapted GRADE (Guyatt et al., 2008), an established framework for evaluating clinical evidence that rates the importance of outcomes on a nine-point scale, with scores of 7-9 indicating outcomes critical to decision-making.

Our results show that major effects (scores 7–9) are flagged in 9.5% of fully reproduced findings (55 of 579). Expert review of 10 flagged cases found that 9 did not establish a consequential change under a defensible alternative, while 1 required further review. Thus, in contrast to the sensitivity reported for the social science datasets studied by Bertran et al. (2026) and Miao et al. (2026), our findings suggest that the medical papers in SEER-Repro exhibit a high degree of robustness to the analytical alternatives tested—an encouraging sign for the reliability of published medical research.

Overall, our results show how LLM agents can strengthen the scientific process by reproducing findings, systematically testing their robustness, and directing expert attention toward potentially consequential analytical choices.

2 Related Work

2.1 Reproduction and Robustness to Analytical Choice in Scientific Research

Multiverse and specification-curve analyses examine results across defensible analytical specifications, while many-analyst studies demonstrate that independent teams can reach different conclusions from the same data and question (Steegen et al., 2016; Simonsohn et al., 2020; Silberzahn et al., 2018). Related efforts test published findings through reproduction and reanalysis: Delios and others (2022) extend archival analyses to new observations, and Brodeur et al. (2026) reproduce analyses and conduct robustness checks for 110 economics and political science articles. These studies motivate assessing both whether a finding can be reproduced and whether it survives alternative analytical choices. In this work, we investigate whether an LLM-assisted pipeline can help with this important scientific problem.

Recent work automates robustness exploration with AI agents. Bertran et al. (2026) generate analyses with multiple AI analysts and screen their methodological validity with an AI analysis agent. Miao et al. (2026) sample agent-generated specifications and estimate how often defensible paths produce claims at least as extreme as the reported finding. Such analytical variation can reflect subjective judgments about how to operationalize a research question. We investigate how this problem manifests in medical epidemiology, where choices about cancer cohorts, outcome definitions, and statistical analyses can alter findings relevant to clinical practice and public health.

2.2 Data-Driven Deep Research Benchmarks and Evaluation

Deep-research benchmarks such as DeepResearchBench, ReportBench, and DeepScholar-Bench assess report quality, evidence coverage, and citation grounding (Du et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Patel et al., 2025). Data-oriented benchmarks evaluate insight generation and executable scientific workflows, including InsightBench, DiscoveryBench, and ScienceAgentBench (Sahu et al., 2025; Majumder et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). BLADE additionally evaluates conceptual variables, transformations, and models across multiple valid analyses (Gu et al., 2024). DataSTORM, Hunt, and DAgent extend this setting to database investigation and report generation (Liu et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2025). Our evaluation asks whether a report’s conclusions survive defensible changes to the analytical choices that produced them, using executed alternatives linked to individual findings. This report-level assessment of analytical robustness is not covered by these prior benchmarks and evaluations.

3 Methodology

3.1 Automated Pipeline for Reproducing Published Findings

In this section, we provide an overview of our proposed agent for reproducing published scientific findings. Our process starts with the paper pp that we are interested in reproducing:

Extract findings and atomic claims: First, we extract the empirical findings Fp={f1,…,fm}F_{p}=\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}\}. These findings represent the core contributions of the paper and underpin the conclusion it draws. We exclude sections of the paper pertaining to related work, background context, or methodology. Each finding fif_{i} is then decomposed into a set of atomic claims Ai={ai​j}j=1niA_{i}=\{a_{ij}\}_{j=1}^{n_{i}}. One atomic claim involves one specific numerical or qualitative target while one finding could group multiple atomic claims together. For instance, “Among women with adenoid cystic carcinoma of the breast, the mean age at diagnosis was 63 years, the median was 62 years, and the range was 33–97 years” is a finding, while its individual targets such as “Among women with adenoid cystic carcinoma of the breast, the mean age at diagnosis was 63 years” (and similarly for “median age: 62 years” and “age range: 33–97 years”) each become a separate atomic claim.

Reproduce findings: We then ask a coding agent to reproduce each finding fif_{i} using the original paper pp, the data used by the paper, and any additional documentation for the data. The agent identifies the relevant data, writes analysis code, and executes it to produce evidence eie_{i} for whether the finding can be validated or not. The evidence eie_{i} includes the output of any analytical code and its results.

Grade individual claims: Finally, for each atomic claim and evidence pair (ai​j,ei)(a_{ij},e_{i}), a claim verification agent checks the method, extracts the reproduced result, and assesses the quantitative or qualitative agreement with the known target values in ai​ja_{ij} to produce a final verdict vi​j∈{Reproduced,Close,NotReproduced}v_{ij}\in\{\textsc{Reproduced},\textsc{Close},\textsc{NotReproduced}\}. For numerical targets, we consider a claim reproduced if the relative error is at most 5%, while errors greater than 5% and at most 10% are counted as close. Qualitative claims are deemed either reproduced or not reproduced. The full protocol for grading is presented in Appendix F.

3.2 Analytical Robustness Analysis

The reproduction artifacts, including the exact code derived, then serve as a foundation for analytic robustness evaluation. Our overall approach uses 3 complementary methods illustrated in Figure 2.

3.2.1 Independent Report Generation

Our first method asks whether an independent analysis of the same research question would reach a conclusion that contradicts the original paper (Figure 2 (A)). For each paper pp, a coding agent receives a research question specifying the topic and scope derived from pp, together with access to relevant data and additional documentation about the data, if available, and is tasked with independently answering the research question. The agent chooses its analytical approach, writes and executes code, and produces a research report rr. We then judge whether the conclusions in rr contradict those in pp. Appendix C documents the report-generation setup and the prompts for all 20 research questions.

3.2.2 Perturbation Agent

Our second method uses the Perturbation Agent illustrated in Figure 2 (B) and Algorithm 1. Appendix D details the implementation of each component, including prompts.

Eligible findings. For a published paper pp, we start from the findings reproduced according to Section 3.1:

Fprep={fi∈Fp:vi​j​ is reproduced for every ​ai​j∈Ai}.F^{\mathrm{rep}}_{p}=\{f_{i}\in F_{p}:v_{ij}\text{ is reproduced for every }a_{ij}\in A_{i}\}. (1)

Only fully reproduced findings enter the robustness analysis: their reconstructed results have passed the reproduction criteria in Section 3.1, and their reproduction code provides the baseline for testing alternative analytical choices.

SelectAnalyticalChoices: First, the pipeline identifies analytical choices made in pp that contribute to the known outcome for the findings FprepF^{\mathrm{rep}}_{p}, such as cohort definitions, endpoints, or statistical models. The set ℛp\mathcal{R}_{p} of independent reports generated for pp is used as an additional reference. These choices are then ordered by scientific importance and feasibility to select up to 20 choices which form the final set of choices 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p}.

ProposeAlternatives: Next, the pipeline establishes how the paper pp implements each selected choice in 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p}, using the reproduction evidence Ep={ei}i=1mE_{p}=\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, where eie_{i} contains the evidence for finding fif_{i}. It then proposes defensible alternatives. The resulting set 𝒦p\mathcal{K}_{p} contains comparisons (k,s)(k,s), where each k∈𝒞pk\in\mathcal{C}_{p} is a selected analytical choice and ss is a proposed alternative setting.

ExecuteAnalyses: For each comparison (k,s)(k,s), we run the baseline unchanged and validate it against the available evidence. We then apply the alternative choice while holding the remaining analysis fixed.

Assess Consequences: Finally, the pipeline assigns each comparison an outcome yk​(s)y_{k}(s) from the enumerated type

AnalysisOutcome={\displaystyle\texttt{AnalysisOutcome}=\{ DirectChange,Qualification,\displaystyle\texttt{DirectChange},\ \texttt{Qualification}, (2)
StableUnderTest,Inconclusive,\displaystyle\texttt{StableUnderTest},\ \texttt{Inconclusive},
Unavailable,NotTested}.\displaystyle\texttt{Unavailable},\ \texttt{NotTested}\}.

DirectChange denotes a change to a stated finding; Qualification narrows its scope or evidentiary strength without directly changing its conclusion; and StableUnderTest means the completed comparison does not meet the criterion for a consequential change. Inconclusive means the evidence cannot support a verdict, Unavailable indicates missing required inputs or baseline evidence, and NotTested records comparisons excluded before execution.

The outcome label only describes what happens to the tested finding. For DirectChange outcomes, we additionally grade the effect on the source’s conclusions from 1 to 9, using a scale adapted from GRADE’s outcome-importance framework (Guyatt et al., 2008). Scores 1–3 indicate quantitative sensitivity without substantive interpretive change, 4–6 indicate qualifications or changes to secondary findings, and 7–9 indicate major qualification, loss of support, or reversal of a principal conclusion.

3.2.3 Direct Coding Agent Analysis

Our third method asks a coding agent to identify and test consequential analytical choices directly (Figure 2 (C)). For each paper, the agent receives the paper pp, the available reproduction evidence EpE_{p}, and access to the data and data documentation when available. We then instruct the agent to select scientifically defensible alternatives addressing the same research question, validate the baseline analysis, and, where feasible, execute comparisons that vary one choice while holding the remaining analysis fixed (with Prompt 30). It produces a report describing the choices tested, the supporting evidence, and their effects on the source’s conclusions. After the analysis, we grade all output choices using the same 1–9 scale as in Section 3.2.2.

4 Experiments

4.1 SEER-Repro Construction Challenges

We apply our pipeline to published SEER findings. Reconstructing these studies presents two challenges:

Historical data availability. Detroit was excluded from the April 2022 release, changing SEER 9, 13, and 18 to SEER 8, 12, and 17 (National Cancer Institute, 2026c). We focus on SEER 9 studies because a retained supplement covers 1975–2018, including Detroit (National Cancer Institute, 2026d). Current releases cannot recover the exact historical SEER 13 and 18 cohorts. Appendix A details remaining limitations.

Fragmented data and documentation. Epidemiological studies often rely on external population data and relevant manuals. We curate these resources manually through an iterative process with expert input. Missing inputs often become apparent only as individual analyses are reconstructed, and identifying what is missing can itself require tracing the analysis step by step. For example, reproducing an incidence rate requires identifying an appropriate population denominator, locating its source, and checking that its geographic coverage, calendar years, and demographic definitions match the cancer records. Selecting among candidate sources also requires assessing their suitability and consulting the relevant manuals. This process therefore requires manual curation and expert judgment, rather than simply retrieving a known list of files.

We curated SEER 9 case table, four county-population tables, 34 SEER*Explorer tables, and associated documentation on coding, staging, registry mappings, and population methods (Appendix B). These 39 tables contain a combined 713 columns and 198,255,448 rows (Table 6). The accompanying 40 documentation resources include 11 PDF manuals and reference documents totaling 816 pages, 28 web pages, and one variable-dictionary spreadsheet (Table 5). These data tables and documentation resources form the execution environment for SEER-Repro.

4.2 SEER-Repro Benchmark and Reproduction Outcome

We collect the ten most cited eligible papers and ten more recent papers in SEER-Repro. Using GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh via Codex, our reproduction agent reproduces 1,694 of 2,190 atomic claims (77.4%); 76 are close (3.5%) and 420 are not reproduced (19.2%; Table 1). We classify the 420 failures using Prompt 6 and review the diagnoses against saved evidence. Data issues account for 251 (59.8%), insufficiently specified analyses for 47 (11.2%), unavailable-software approximations for 28 (6.7%), and agent-side errors for 48 (11.4%; Table 2).

The benchmark packages 39 data tables and 40 documentation resources (Appendix B), together with the 2,190 atomic claims over 20 papers. Each claim ai​j∈Aia_{ij}\in A_{i} links to its paper pp, parent finding fif_{i}, verdict vi​jv_{ij}, and reproduction evidence eie_{i}, including code and available execution outputs.

4.3 Robustness Analysis of SEER-Repro

4.3.1 Independent Report Generation

For each paper, we independently ask Opus 4.8 max via Claude Code and GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh via Codex to generate a report. GPT-5.6 Sol then compares each of the 40 reports with its corresponding paper for contradictions on their shared research question (Prompt 1). The judge identifies no contradictions in the central conclusions of the 39 comparable reports (19 Sol and 20 Opus). One Sol report analyzes a nonoverlapping study period and is not comparable. It marked 3 Opus reports as containing contradictions in supporting statements, but these do not overturn their central conclusions upon closer scrutiny. These results suggest that independent analyses generally reach central conclusions non-contradictory with the published papers.

4.3.2 Perturbation Agent and Direct Coding Agent Analysis

We run the Perturbation Agent with GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026), Opus 4.8 (Anthropic, 2026), Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026), and GLM 5.3 (Z.ai, 2026), together with direct coding agent analyses through GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh via Codex and Opus 4.8 max via Claude Code. These correspond to methods B and C in Figure 2. GPT-5.6 Sol then assigned scores of 7–9 to 54 results (Prompt 31). These scores indicate a model-assessed major qualification, loss of support, or reversal of a principal conclusion and help identify shortlisted candidates for expert examination.

We use GPT-5.6 Sol to link these high-score results back to the original findings in each paper (Prompt 32). A model-assessed consequential link requires reported evidence of a reversal, loss of support, major qualification, or material change to a quantity central to one specific finding or a conclusion that the paper draws jointly from multiple findings. In the latter case, we link the analysis to each supporting finding. Table 3 shows that 55 of the 579 fully reproduced findings (9.5%) have such a link from at least one analyst, and 14 (2.4%) from at least two analysts.

Discussion: As mentioned in Section 3.2, we restrict this analysis to fully reproduced findings. This provides executable baselines whose results passed the reproduction criteria in Section 3.1. The analysts can therefore compare an alternative against a reconstructed result supported by reproduction evidence. We further consider two questions:

Do different analysts complement each other? Results in Table 3 show that most of the affected findings—41 of 55 (74.5%)—are identified by only one analyst. This suggests that different analysts identify largely complementary sets of potentially consequential analytical choices.

Distribution of consequence scores. Among results with a 1–9 grade (Figure 3), scores 7–9 account for 7.5–14.8% of Perturbation Agent comparisons, 19.4% of Codex results, and 17.4% of Claude Code results. Thus, most graded results do not reach the high-consequence range.

4.3.3 Expert Analysis

One coauthor with medical expertise and familiarity with SEER data manually examined 10 cases scored 7–9 in depth (five each from Perturbation Agent and Direct Coding Agent Analysis). Among the 5 cases from the Perturbation Agent, 2 suggested consequential changes, but closer expert scrutiny indicated that the alternatives were likely less defensible than the original analytical choices; the remaining 3 offered only limited qualifications to the papers’ conclusions. Among the 5 cases from direct coding agent analysis, 4 likewise offered only limited qualifications. The remaining 1 case identified a potentially overstated comparison between nasal and non-nasal incidence trends, but determining its consequence requires closer manuscript review and statistical consultation. Thus, 9 cases did not establish a consequential change under a defensible alternative, while 1 remains flagged for further review. Table 4 illustrates 3 cases with one from each category: a likely less defensible alternative, a limited qualification to the paper’s conclusions, and a potentially consequential issue requiring further review.

Overall, our pipeline narrows the material requiring expert attention by autonomously reconstructing published findings, executing alternative analyses, and prioritizing potentially consequential results. Across 579 fully reproduced findings, it identifies 55 with model-assessed consequential links, providing a focused shortlist and supporting evidence for expert review. Experts can therefore concentrate on whether the flagged alternatives are scientifically defensible and will materially change the conclusions, rather than reconstructing and testing each analysis from scratch manually.

5 Conclusion

We introduced SEER-Repro, a benchmark of 20 published SEER studies, and an AI-assisted pipeline for evaluating reproducibility and robustness to analytical choices. Our reproduction agent recovered 77.4% of atomic claims. Automated robustness assessments then prioritized 55 of 579 fully reproduced findings (9.5%) for expert review, providing a focused shortlist with supporting analytical evidence. Expert examination of 10 flagged cases clarified why 9 did not establish consequential changes under defensible alternatives and identified 1 potentially consequential issue requiring further investigation. These results illustrate how automated analysis can focus expert attention on questions that warrant closer scientific scrutiny.

SEER provides an early, high-stakes testbed for this approach. Longer term, such checks could become part of scientific infrastructure: published findings could be routinely reassessed as data, methods, and analytical alternatives evolve, with potentially consequential sensitivities prioritized for expert review.

AI Use Statement

Uses of generative AI. In this work, we used generative AI tools to help develop theoretical models or conceptual frameworks; propose or refine hypotheses; design or provide feedback on research methodology or experiments; implement methods; clean and reformat datasets; support qualitative and thematic data analysis; interpret results; create or modify scientific figures or images; create or edit software code; draft parts of the paper; create artifacts; summarize or analyze existing literature; discover research topics or identify gaps; brainstorm; source and search for information; improve the paper’s readability; identify relevant literature; and format references.

Activities without generative AI. We did not use generative AI tools to suggest experimental parameters, suggest a structure for the paper, or propose a title or keywords.

Activities not applicable to this work. Generating synthetic datasets, formulating mathematical claims, providing critical ingredients for mathematical proofs, assisting with proof writing, translating, formulating survey or interview questions, and transcribing research recordings are not applicable to this work.

Additional disclosure and author responsibility. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. For example, the final writing has been double-checked by authors. We have reviewed all relevant literature manually found by LLMs. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Ethics Statement

This work aims to support scientific reliability by evaluating the reproducibility and analytical robustness of published cancer epidemiology findings. We acknowledge that errors in our pipeline, including but not limited to data selection, LLM-generated code, interpretation, and grading, may lead to incorrect assessments. Failure to reproduce a finding may also reflect unavailable historical data (as documented in Section 4.1). Sensitivity to an alternative analysis does not invalidate the original study and requires careful expert judgment to assess its significance (as discussed in Section 4). Our goal is to help experts identify findings that warrant closer examination, making rigorous scientific review more accessible while keeping expert judgment central to the process.

Reproducibility Statement

We document the SEER data releases and registry coverage in Appendix A, and the database resources, manuals, source links, and file formats in Appendix B. Table 1 identifies the exact 20 papers evaluated in SEER-Repro. Appendix C provides the research prompts and report-generation settings, while Appendix D describes the analysis implementation and Appendix H provides the LLM prompts. Section 4 identifies the tested analysis models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Opus 4.8, GLM 5.3, and Kimi K3) and the coding-agent configurations used in the comparison experiments.

Appendix

Appendix A SEER Data Evolution and Study Scope

Registry Overview.

SEER 9, SEER 13, and SEER 18 identify different geographic cohorts, with standard diagnosis-year coverage beginning in 1975, 1992, and 2000, respectively. Figure 4 summarizes their expansion and subsequent changes. With the November 2021 submission, released in April 2022, Detroit was excluded from the new databases, yielding SEER 8, 12, and 17. Massachusetts was subsequently excluded from the November 2024 submission, changing SEER 22 to SEER 21 (National Cancer Institute, 2026c; National Cancer Institute, 2026b).

Why we focus on SEER 9?

The supplemental November 2020 database preserves SEER 9 records, including Detroit, through 2018. We use this retained cohort and select papers whose analyses do not require additional registries. It is in general difficult to reconstruct historical SEER 13 and SEER 18 datasets using the newer, Detroit-excluding releases (SEER 12 and SEER 17), since each case does not record the exact associated registry.

Release and variable differences remain.

Retaining the registry grouping does not guarantee identical historical inputs. For example, the November 2020 submission changed the default malignant-behavior definition and excluded approximately 10,000 previously included, no-longer-reportable borderline cases, predominantly ovarian tumors (National Cancer Institute, 2026a). Our local failure diagnostics also identify unavailable radiation-treatment fields, preventing reconstruction of some treatment proportions even when registry coverage matches. We retain these limitations when interpreting claim-level reproduction outcomes. For instance, these cases would count towards “Data Issues” in Table 2.

Appendix B Supplementary SEER Tables and Manuals

The curated SEER-Repro environment contains the SEER 9 case table, 4 population denominator tables, 34 SEER*Explorer aggregate tables, and 40 documentation files or reference pages.

Population denominators.

The four population tables provide county-level annual estimates by age, sex, and race, with an expanded race/Hispanic-origin scheme available from 1990. Each series is supplied both in 20 age groups and in single-year ages through 89 with a 90+ category (Table 6). These are all-state files: rates for a SEER cohort require restricting them to the corresponding registry counties (National Cancer Institute, 2026f).

SEER*Explorer aggregates.

We include 34 workbooks from the official November 2024 SEER*Explorer archive as queryable tables. Table 6 lists each table with its column count, row count, and description. They supplement case-level computation with aggregated statistics.

Manuals and reference definitions.

Table 5 lists the 40 documentation resources supplied in SEER-Repro: 28 HTML pages, 11 PDFs, and one XLSX spreadsheet. The collection covers SEER*Stat dictionaries, population denominators and standardization, coding and staging, variable recodes, and registry coverage. It includes both recent manuals and a historical-manual index.

Appendix C Details on LLM-Generated Research Reports

For each of the 20 cases in SEER-Repro, we supply the same neutral research prompt to two coding agents: Claude Code with Opus at the maximum effort setting, and Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol at the xhigh effort setting. Both agents have access to all databases and manuals included in SEER-Repro. The prompts specify the research topic and scope without supplying the published findings. Table 7 lists the exact neutral prompt used for each case.

Appendix D Perturbation Agent: Implementation Details

We implement the components in Section 3.2.2 with LLM calls and coding agents. This appendix describes their inputs, prompts, configuration, and the validation controls applied at each stage. Section 4 reports the models evaluated. Our experiments include a published paper and Sol- and Opus-generated reports (Appendix C) for each research question.

The semantic-call wrapper can request a corrected complete JSON object after schema or parsing failures (Prompt 29).

Select Analytical Choices (Step 1). For each published paper pp, we identify candidate analytical choices relevant to its fully reproduced findings FprepF^{\mathrm{rep}}_{p}. An LLM receives the paper, eligible findings, and reproduction evidence EpE_{p}, and extracts choices such as cohort definitions, endpoints, subgroup definitions, statistical models, and interpretation rules (Prompt 7). For each generated report r∈ℛpr\in\mathcal{R}_{p}, a separate call extracts choices from the report and its available execution log, linking them to the paper’s eligible findings where applicable (Prompt 8). We verify finding identifiers and supporting quotations, attempt to repair invalid candidates (Prompt 9), and remove evidence or candidates that remain ungrounded. The validated candidates from all sources are then pooled: an LLM merges descriptions of the same scientific decision and ranks the resulting choices by scientific importance, uncertainty, feasibility, and redundancy, selecting at most 20 choices before any alternative analysis is run (Prompt 10). Review and repair calls resolve problems with the proposed selection (Prompts 11–15), yielding the finalized choice set 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p} used to propose alternatives.

Propose Alternatives. (Step 2 of the Perturbation Agent in Figure 2) For each selected analytical choice, an LLM examines how each paper or report implements that choice, using the source text and available execution evidence (Prompt 16) and documents the exact setting. Using these original settings and findings, another LLM proposes a defensible alternative to test across sources, adding a second only when it represents a materially different approach (Prompt 18). A separate LLM reviews whether each proposed alternative is scientifically justified and identifies any conditions required for its use before execution (Prompt 20). Choices without a defensible alternative are not tested.

Stage-specific repair calls correct invalid baseline mappings, alternatives, or alternative reviews using the associated validation errors (Prompts 17, 19, and 21). Deterministic checks enforce valid identifiers and complete coverage of the required records.

Execute Analyses. (Step 3 of the Perturbation Agent in Figure 2) For each choice–alternative comparison (k,s)∈𝒦p(k,s)\in\mathcal{K}_{p}, the planning LLM receives the baseline settings, the reviewed alternative, linked findings, feasibility conditions, and execution evidence; it decides whether the comparison should be executed and draws up a concrete plan for its implementation (Prompt 22). Invalid plans are repaired against the validation errors, with deterministic checks of identifiers and comparison coverage (Prompt 23). Executable comparisons are then fed to coding agents for implementation (Prompt 24). The executor first runs the baseline unchanged and checks it against the frozen validation criteria. It then copies the baseline, changes only the specified choice and its listed dependent calculations, and saves the baseline output, alternative output, validation evidence, and exact code diff. These saved artifacts form the comparison evidence ek​(s)e_{k}(s) returned by the Execute Analyses stage in Algorithm 1.

The pipeline prepares the SEER-Repro environment for execution. The launch prompt (Prompt 28) directs the coding agent to follow the execution instructions (Prompt 24). The agent recovers the baseline implementation from preserved code, structured execution traces, or legacy transcripts, in that order of preference; it constructs a fresh implementation only when no prior implementation evidence survives. It then validates the unchanged baseline, executes the specified alternatives, and saves the results and supporting evidence. If a Codex session ends successfully without the required results file, a continuation prompt asks it to finish using the same workspace (Prompt 26). If the file remains missing, a final prompt stops further analysis and requires it to record existing results, marking unfinished comparisons as unavailable (Prompt 27).

Assess Consequences. (Step 4 of the Perturbation Agent in Figure 2) A separate assessment LLM receives each comparison, its eligibility evidence, frozen comparison criteria, and the saved execution evidence ek​(s)e_{k}(s) (Prompt 25). This implements the Assess Consequences stage in Algorithm 1, assigning an outcome yk​(s)y_{k}(s) using the AnalysisOutcome type defined in Equation 2.

For DirectChange outcomes, a further LLM call assigns a scientific-consequence score from 1 to 9 based on the report’s conclusions and the baseline-to-alternative evidence (Prompt 31), adapted from GRADE’s nine-point outcome-importance framework (Guyatt et al., 2008). The score bands are interpreted as described in Section 3.2.2.

Appendix E Reproduction Outcome Breakdowns in SEER-Repro

Table 8 provides the counts and percentages for all three reproduction outcomes for each paper, alongside its numbers of findings and atomic claims.

Table 9 reports the 20-paper breakdown using cumulative 1%, 5%, and 10% tolerances for quantitative claims and binary outcomes for qualitative claims. Of 1,695 quantitative claims, 1,299 are reproduced (76.6%), 76 are close, and 320 are not reproduced. Of 495 qualitative claims, 395 are reproduced (79.8%) and 100 are not reproduced. Together these yield the 1,694 reproduced, 76 close, and 420 not-reproduced claims reported in the main text.

Appendix F Reproduction Grading Details

Findings are extracted (Prompt 2), decomposed into atomic targets (Prompt 3), and attempted to be reproduced (Prompt 4). The reproduction grader separates evidence assessment from numerical comparison. An LLM extracts the result reported for each atomic claim and assesses its method and answer provenance (Prompt 5); deterministic code then applies the numerical grading policy. The reproduction agent’s own statement that a finding was reproduced does not determine the final verdict.

F.1 Judge Inputs and Evidence Assessment

Inputs and unit of assessment. One judge call receives the reproduction report for an original finding together with its atomic targets. Each target includes its identifier, claim text, reference answer, numerical or semantic evaluation mode, verification target, source quotation, and required analytical assumptions. The judge is instructed to assess every atomic target independently: reproducing one component of a finding does not establish that its other components were reproduced. The grading call receives the report and structured targets, rather than independently inspecting the complete code and execution trace or rerunning the analysis.

Result availability. For each target, the judge records whether the requested result is reported, not reported, or unclear. A missing reproduction report is assigned a not-reproduced verdict directly. When a report exists but omits the requested result or provides ambiguous evidence, the target likewise receives no reproduction credit.

Method validity. The judge assesses whether the reported computation uses a valid method for the specific target. This includes compatibility with required cohort bounds, disease and variable coding, outcome measures, grouping, denominators, standardization conventions, temporal data definitions, and statistical-model settings. A conflicting analytical assumption makes the method invalid; insufficient methodological evidence makes it unclear. The report need not repeat every required assumption verbatim, but it must establish a compatible computation. Both invalid and unclear methods lead to a not-reproduced verdict, even when the extracted numerical value matches the reference.

Answer provenance. The judge also flags evidence that the result was obtained by recalling, copying, or searching for the published answer instead of computing it from the supplied data. Such results receive no reproduction credit. Consulting documentation, variable definitions, or coding guidance is permitted when the agent subsequently performs the computation. An exact numerical match alone is not evidence of copying.

F.2 Numerical Extraction and Comparison

Only claims passing the evidence checks in Section F.1 proceed to numerical grading. The process has three steps.

1. Extract the computed result. The LLM extracts each required value, its unit, and its relation (==, <<, ≤\leq, >>, or ≥\geq), using unrounded values when available. It follows the target’s requested representation—for example, distinguishing the magnitude of a decline from a signed change. It does not calculate numerical error or assign the numerical verdict.

2. Compare each required component. For an ordinary point estimate with reference value t≠0t\neq 0 and computed value xx, deterministic code calculates

ε=|x−t||t|.\varepsilon=\frac{|x-t|}{|t|}.

The component is Reproduced if ε≤5%\varepsilon\leq 5\%, Close if 5%<ε≤10%5\%<\varepsilon\leq 10\%, and Not reproduced otherwise. Counts also use this rule unless the target specifies another tolerance.

The following cases modify this default comparison:

Case Comparison rule
Rounding allowance If the target specifies its reported decimal precision, accept differences up to half a unit in the last reported decimal place—for example, 0.050.05 for one decimal place.
Explicit tolerance Use the target’s exact-equality or absolute-error thresholds instead of the default relative thresholds, subject to the rounding allowance.
Zero reference Under the default relative rule, require x=0x=0, unless the rounding allowance applies.
Inequality Check whether the computed value satisfies the target inequality. If only a bound is reported, it must imply the target bound. A bound cannot establish a required point value. These comparisons have no Close category.
Interval For an acceptable range, check whether the computed scalar lies within its boundaries, respecting strict or inclusive limits. For a reported interval, compare its two endpoints separately.

3. Combine the component verdicts. Required components are matched in their declared order; optional uncertainty components are excluded. The least favorable component verdict determines the atomic claim’s verdict. Missing or unparseable required values yield “Not reproduced”.

F.3 Grading Qualitative Claims

For qualitative or categorical claims, the judge determines whether the reproduced result supports the same conclusion as the published claim. A claim is marked reproduced only when the conclusions are equivalent and the evidence passes the availability, method-validity, and answer-provenance checks described above. Approximately equivalent, conflicting, or unclear conclusions are marked not reproduced. Unlike numerical claims, qualitative claims have no close category.

Implementation checks and saved records.

The implementation verifies that the judge returns the requested claim identifiers and that extracted numerical results have the required structure. Saved records include the extracted result, assessment fields, rationale, final verdict, and grading-policy version. Numerical thresholds can therefore be reapplied to saved extractions without another judge call. Table 9 reports outcomes by claim type.

Scope of the grades.

These grades assess whether the reproduction report provides sufficient evidence for the original claim. They do not independently verify the complete analysis code or establish that undocumented analytical choices match those of the original authors.
